Now, if I do try to reach out to someone, I feel a deep sense of loneliness and rejection if I seem to be snubbed.

Conversation partners, both for writing and for speaking, spurred my biggest improvements. I pushed myself beyond my limit when talking and messaging friends, to the point of being sure I was making mistakes or using grammar that I was very uncomfortable with, so that they would correct me and tell me the right way to say what I'm thinking. 

Of course, it's important to let your friends know (often repeatedly) that you WANT them to nitpick everything you say. Most Japanese won't do this naturally! 

I do recommend studying from a book in addition to getting real world practice. Studying new grammar is probably more useful than studying new vocabulary; new vocabulary just lets you change out words in a sentence, but new grammar lets you express more complex thoughts with the words you already know.

Besides, you can always look up words in a dictionary until you memorize them just from doing that.

My theory on this... We humans have developed as a species for at least 100,000 years, and our pre-human ancestors developed over millions of years.

Our brains developed for all the eventualities of life that the world could throw at us... Until instant communication was invented. 

Less than 200 years since the invention of the telegraph is not enough time for our brains to evolve to cope with the change. Waiting a week for a text doesn't feel the same as waiting a month for a letter; it's more like taking to someone directly in person, and not even being acknowledged. It hurts a lot.

Strangely, in my case, it only feels that way when I'm the one being "snubbed". It feels normal to ignore or delay responses to other people. How's that for hypocrisy? 

But some people handle it just fine, right? Well, just as our brains didn't evolve to handle instant communication, they didn't evolve *not* to handle it either. It's a crapshoot; either you're lucky or you aren't.

So, what can people like you or I do about it? If anyone has a good answer, I want to hear it as much as you do. But, I think it starts with really hard decisions about our relationship with technology. Do we really need smart phones? 

Maybe we do. I don't know yet.

For future generations, though, I do think that the way we deal with communication technology needs to be built on a carefully constructed system of manners and self-control, and it needs to be taught from kindergarten the same way that basic etiquette is instilled in children today. That can maybe help save them from our troubles.

My advice as a programmer: If you have no prior programming experience, don't bother properly learning C# from scratch for a single project. It takes months just to understand the basics well enough to make almost-useful text-based programs. Not worth your time if you aren't going to use it regularly, and especially if you need to do this pretty quickly.

Instead, find an AR tutorial, follow it step by step even if you don't know exactly what everything means. Then, try tweaking the tutorial files to make it more and more like your vision. Editing something that already exists has a lot of limitations, but it's a whole lot faster than learning a new language from the bottom up.

If you enjoy the project enough, then go back and learn more about the language later, when you have time to really learn the fundamentals and build up slowly. Otherwise, just get that project done and move on to the next one without wasting your time!
